articles.title: The bipartisan energy bill tearing the climate movement apart
articles.author: Austin Corona
articles.summary: In order to solve climate change, you have to do two things — stop burning fossil fuels, and build clean energy to replace them. The last few decades in the United States have witnessed a long back-and-forth over which of the two goals is more important, and over how to achieve either of them. Is it more important to pass a carbon tax, or subsidize electric vehicles? To block a new oil pipeline, or build a lot of solar and wind? On this question, the coalition known as the climate movement has fractured into two broad groups. On one side, there are activists, lawyers, and environmentalists, who tend to focus on blocking and reducing fossil fuel use. On the other, there are renewable energy companies and policy wonks, who tend to focus on building more clean energy. These factions have clashed in the past, but over the past week a kind of civil war has erupted between the different elements of the climate movement. articles.author: Drew Berkemeyer
articles.summary: Hurricane Isaias weakened into a post-tropical cyclone Saturday after making landfall along Florida’s Gulf Coast, but not before the storm killed at least two people, damaged homes, and knocked out electricity for hundreds of thousands of people across the Southeast. The storm made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening as a Category 2 hurricane, packing maximum sustained winds of 105 mph. It moved north through the Florida Panhandle and into Alabama, where its winds weakened sharply. By early Saturday, Isaias had maximum sustained winds of about 35 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center . At least two people were killed when trees fell on their homes, one in Florida and another in Alabama, authorities said. The Escambia County Sheriff’s Office in Florida reported that a woman died when a tree struck her home. In Jefferson County, Alabama, emergency management officials reported a second fatality after a tree fell on a house. Officials had not released further details about the victims. The storm also caused widespread damage across the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama. Strong winds toppled trees and power lines, damaged buildings, and left roads hazardous.

stories.summary: MANDEL NGAN / AFP via Getty Images President Donald Trump’s attempt to ban news outlets he doesn’t like has taken another extraordinary turn: the Justice Department is now reportedly investigating the television networks that pushed back against him. The DOJ—which is headed up by Trump’s former personal attorney, Todd Blanche—has launched an antitrust investigation into ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC, and even Fox News after the five networks temporarily suspended their shared coverage of the president in protest at his decision to bar three news organizations from the White House, The New York Times reported Saturday. The newest escalation comes after Trump’s press crackdown backfired spectacularly last month, leaving the White House scrambling to get cameras back into presidential events. Read more at The Daily Beast.
